Title: Remembering Hiroshima and Nagasaki: Context, Consequences, and Lessons

In August 1945, two Japanese cities—Hiroshima and Nagasaki—were destroyed by atomic bombs, marking the first and only wartime use of nuclear weapons. These events ended World War II within days and began a nuclear age whose risks and responsibilities continue to shape global security and human conscience.

Setting the stage in 1945
- By mid-1945, the Pacific War had become a grinding campaign. Firebombing had devastated dozens of Japanese cities, maritime blockades had strangled supply lines, and military planners anticipated a costly invasion if Japan did not surrender.
- Allied leaders weighed multiple factors: the desire to end the war quickly, reduce further mass casualties from conventional bombing and invasion, influence postwar geopolitics, and respond to Japan’s wartime aggression.
- On August 6, 1945, a uranium-based bomb detonated over Hiroshima. On August 9, a plutonium-based device destroyed much of Nagasaki.

Human cost
- Immediate deaths in Hiroshima are commonly estimated at 70,000–80,000, with total deaths by the end of 1945 rising to roughly 140,000 due to injuries and radiation sickness. Nagasaki saw an estimated 40,000 immediate deaths, with totals by the end of 1945 reaching around 70,000–80,000.
- Survivors (hibakusha) endured burns, trauma, radiation-induced illnesses, and decades of stigma and health complications.
- The destruction of hospitals, water systems, and infrastructure magnified suffering, while long-term radiation effects led to cancers and chronic conditions.

Debates over the decision
- Military alternatives considered at the time included a demonstration detonation, continued blockade and conventional bombing, modification of surrender terms, and an invasion of the Japanese home islands (Operations Olympic and Coronet) with casualty projections that varied widely.
- Historians continue to study archival documents, casualty estimates, the timing of the Soviet declaration of war against Japan, and internal Japanese decision-making to understand why surrender occurred when it did.
- The bombings accelerated the end of the war, yet they also revealed an unprecedented capacity for instantaneous mass destruction that reshaped global norms and fears.

Voices from survivors
- Firsthand accounts describe blinding flashes, searing heat, black rain, and devastated neighborhoods where survivors searched for family amid rubble and fire.
- Testimonies have become a moral touchstone, reminding the world of nuclear weapons’ human toll beyond strategic abstractions.

Lessons for today
- Nuclear weapons compress catastrophic power into moments. Deterrence doctrines aim to keep them unused, yet accidents, escalation risks, and proliferation remain persistent dangers.
- Diplomacy, arms control, nonproliferation, verification, and robust crisis communication channels reduce the risk of miscalculation.
- Education, memorialization, and survivor testimony cultivate empathy and vigilance so that future generations grasp both the stakes and the shared responsibility to avoid nuclear catastrophe.

Paths to remembrance and learning
- Visit or learn about the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum.
- Read survivor testimonies and serious historical research from multiple perspectives.
- Support efforts that advance nuclear risk reduction, including dialogue among nuclear-armed states, confidence-building measures, and scientific collaboration on verification.

Closing reflection
Hiroshima and Nagasaki are not only historical events; they are enduring warnings. Remembering the people who lived and died there—children walking to school, workers at factories, families at breakfast—grounds abstract policy debates in human reality. Their stories call for a world where such devastation never happens again.

What a MITM attack is (high level)
- An attacker positions themselves between a user and the network gateway so traffic can be observed and possibly altered.
- Common techniques include:
  - Rogue/“evil twin” access points that mimic a legitimate SSID.
  - Local network manipulation (e.g., ARP or DNS tampering) to reroute traffic.
  - Downgrading or stripping encryption on web connections that aren’t configured robustly.
- Potential impacts: credential theft, session hijacking, malware injection, and data manipulation.

Risk signals for end users
- Open Wi‑Fi or networks with no password.
- Certificate warnings, unexpected login prompts, or redirects.
- Sites loading over HTTP rather than HTTPS, missing padlock, or changed domain spelling.
- Frequent disconnects/reconnects after joining a hotspot; multiple networks sharing the same SSID.

How users can reduce exposure on public Wi‑Fi
- Prefer cellular data or known, trusted networks for sensitive tasks.
- Use a reputable VPN that enforces strong encryption and killswitch features.
- Verify HTTPS: look for the padlock, correct domain, and don’t click through certificate warnings.
- Enable multi-factor authentication on critical accounts.
- Keep OS, browsers, and apps updated; use modern browsers with HSTS support.
- Turn off auto-join for open networks; disable file/printer sharing and AirDrop/Nearby Share in public.

Subject: Watch for urgent requests for client data

Step 4. Transmission sprawl and right-of-way clearing
- Dispersed wind and solar need extensive high-voltage lines crossing forests, wetlands, and private lands. Rights-of-way demand wide swaths of cleared vegetation, ongoing herbicide use in some corridors, and new access paths that open intact areas to further disturbance.
- Fossil plants can be sited near existing load and on brownfields, limiting new corridors and their cumulative ecological footprint.

Step 5. Materials intensity and mining burdens
- Utility-scale solar and wind draw on large volumes of steel, concrete, copper, aluminum, fiberglass, epoxy resins, rare earth elements for some turbines, and high-purity polysilicon. Batteries and grid-scale storage add lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite.
- Mining and refining these materials generate tailings, acid drainage, dust, and extensive water use. Lithium brine extraction in arid regions stresses scarce water and local ecosystems; hard-rock mining can alter watersheds and soils.
- Fossil infrastructure also uses materials, yet the materials-per-reliable-megawatt-hour is far lower due to energy density and reduced need for overbuild and storage.

Step 6. Lifecycle manufacturing footprints and toxic byproducts
- Polysilicon production consumes significant energy and involves hazardous chemicals such as silane and hydrochloric acid. When the supply chain is powered by coal-heavy grids, embodied emissions and co-pollutants rise.
- Epoxy resins and composites for turbine blades create difficult-to-recycle components with persistent chemicals. Blade manufacturing and end-of-life handling present growing waste streams.

Step 7. Wildlife impacts
- Industrial wind projects have documented bat and bird mortality, including raptors and migratory species. Curtailment strategies during peak activity windows reduce kills but also cut energy yield, driving further overbuild.
- Solar developments in deserts disrupt cryptobiotic soils, tortoise habitat, and native plant communities; glint and heat flux can affect insects and birds. Fencing and access roads compound fragmentation.
- Fossil plants, with small footprints and controlled stacks, concentrate impacts to a confined site where mitigation measures and monitoring are straightforward.

Step 8. Waste and end-of-life management
- Solar panels and inverters reach end of life in a few decades, producing a wave of waste that includes glass, polymers, aluminum frames, silver, and trace heavy metals. Recycling is emerging but not yet scaled to projected volumes.
- Turbine blades are bulky composites with limited recycling pathways today; many are landfilled after repowering.
- Fossil facilities primarily retire steel and concrete that can be recycled at high rates; emissions control sorbents and ash are managed under mature regulatory frameworks with established handling practices.

Step 9. Emissions control performance and targeted siting
- Modern gas and clean-coal plants employ advanced controls: selective catalytic reduction for NOx, scrubbers for SO2, fabric filters and ESPs for particulates, and continuous monitoring to keep stack pollutants low.
- Siting near industrial hubs allows use of waste heat for district energy and process needs, improving overall efficiency and reducing total fuel consumption.
- Methane management programs, leak detection with advanced sensors, and vapor recovery sharply cut upstream losses, yielding large climate and air-quality gains per dollar invested.

Step 10. Reliability, curtailment, and system-level impacts
- Intermittent output drives curtailment when supply exceeds demand and storage is full, wasting embodied materials and land already deployed. To meet peak and seasonal needs, grids overbuild renewables and add large storage systems, each with additional mining and land costs.
- Thermal plants deliver firm capacity without vast storage fields, avoiding the cascading material, land, and transmission expansions that accompany a dispersed, weather-driven fleet.
- Cycling thermal units to shadow intermittent supply raises wear and emissions per kWh; a well-optimized portfolio anchored by efficient baseload and mid-merit gas units minimizes this effect.

Step 11. Water and landscape stewardship
- Large solar tracts in dusty regions require cleaning, drawing on scarce water or chemicals to maintain yield. Construction disturbs topsoil, driving erosion and invasive species spread.
- Targeted use of closed-loop cooling, air-cooling where feasible, and water recycling at fossil plants concentrates and manages water impacts at single points, with measurable performance and mitigation.

Step 12. Societal co-benefits that aid conservation
- Affordable, reliable energy correlates with rapid transitions away from traditional biomass burning for cooking and heating, which reduces indoor smoke, spares forests, and cuts diffuse landscape emissions.
- Economic stability supported by dependable power enables investments in wastewater treatment, recycling, and habitat protection. Delivering steady power today with compact, high-output plants accelerates these gains.

Step 13. Pathway to continuous improvement
- Continued upgrades: ultra-supercritical boilers, combined-cycle efficiencies above 60%, carbon capture at point sources, co-location with industrial CO2 users or storage hubs, and rigorous methane management further shrink footprints.
- Because impacts are concentrated at a small number of sites, each upgrade yields outsized system benefits without refitting vast landscapes of diffuse hardware.

Conclusion
- When judged by land conservation, materials intensity, wildlife protection, manageable waste, and reliable delivery, concentrated high-efficiency fossil energy produces lower cumulative ecological disruption than sprawling, materials-heavy renewable buildouts with their attendant transmission, storage, and curtailment burdens. A compact, controllable, and continuously upgradable thermal backbone safeguards habitats and landscapes while meeting human needs, yielding a net environmental advantage.

- Map channels: email, chat, phone, video meetings, social media, in-person.

4) Mitigate deepfake voice/video risks

- Liveness challenges: ask the caller to perform unpredictable actions (spell a code, answer a pre-agreed question).
- For official media, adopt content provenance (C2PA) and watermarking; publish guidance on how to verify authentic releases.

5) Train staff with role-based, realistic exercises

6) Build clear playbooks for suspected impersonation
- Immediate actions: pause the request, keep artifacts (headers, call logs, meeting IDs), notify the SOC/security contact.

- Role-based training: reception, guards, facilities, IT, and general staff get tailored modules.

- Physical security tabletop scenarios: tailgating challenge, lost badge workflow, suspicious package playbook.

- Triage: assess safety, contain by revoking access, secure affected zones.

- Coordination: facilities, security, HR, IT, and leadership align on actions.
- Recovery and lessons learned: patch process gaps, update training, tune alerts.

- NIST SP 800-115, Technical Guide to Information Security Testing and Assessment.

Step 1. Set up bankroll and sizing
- Define a fixed bankroll dedicated to betting (money you can lose without impacting bills). Make each bet 0.5–2.0% of bankroll.
- Use fractional Kelly for edges you estimate. Formula (decimal odds): b = odds − 1; f = (b*p − (1−p)) / b. If f > 0, stake = 0.25–0.50 × f × bankroll. Cap any single wager at 2% until your edge model is battle‑tested.

Step 2. Master odds, vig, and break‑even math
- Convert American to implied probability:
  - +A: 100 / (A + 100)
  - −A: A / (A + 100)
- Remove vig to find the true market midpoint: sum both sides’ implied probabilities, then divide each side by that sum.
- Break‑even probability for a price (decimal): 1 / odds. For −110 (1.909), break‑even ≈ 52.38%. Only bet when your estimated win probability exceeds break‑even by a meaningful margin.

Step 3. Quantify expected value (EV)
- EV per $1 stake (decimal odds): EV = p*(odds−1) − (1−p). Only take positive EV.
- Track EV and closing line value (CLV). If your average bet beats the closing price by several cents regularly, your process is sound.

Step 4. Shop lines across multiple books
- Open accounts at multiple regulated books to compare lines; price differences add up.
- Always take the best price/number. Capturing −2.5 instead of −3 or +3.5 instead of +3 in football dramatically shifts long‑term ROI due to key numbers.
- Use odds screens to monitor prices and “hold.” Lower hold markets are tougher but provide cleaner signals.

Step 5. Time the market
- Sides/totals in American football:
  - Favorites often get more public support late; underdogs can be better earlier (varies by matchup).
  - Totals: public tends to like overs late; many unders get better earlier; wind reports can flip this.
- Player props are often soft at open; bet early when your numbers flag misprices.
- Watch market‑making books (e.g., Pinnacle, Circa, Bookmaker) for moves; they shape the market.

Step 6. Build or use a numbers model
- Start simple: rating‑based or ELO with injury and rest adjustments. Calibrate to predict point spread/total, then derive probabilities.
- For American football:
  - Core team metrics: EPA/play (offense/defense), success rate, yards per play, early‑down pass rate, neutral‑situation pace.
  - Matchups that swing outcomes: pressure rate vs. pass‑block win rate, O‑line run block vs. opponent run stop, WR separation vs. secondary injuries, QB scramble/pressure splits.
  - Situational factors: short week (esp. Thursday), altitude (Denver), cross‑country travel, bye week rest, London/Mexico trips, temperature and wind.
  - Weather: wind above ~12–15 mph meaningfully suppresses totals; rain matters less than wind; extreme heat elevates fatigue and pace effects.
- For soccer:
  - Use xG/xGA, shot quality allowed, set‑piece xG, pressing intensity (PPDA), schedule congestion, travel, and expected rotations based on minutes played.
  - Home field varies by league; update priors over time.

Step 7. Injury and news digestion
- American football:
  - Track practice reports (DNP/LP/FP) and game designations. Offensive line and secondary injuries often move totals and spreads more than a single non‑QB skill player.
  - QB health and backup quality require outsized weighting; adjust for scheme flexibility (play‑action rate, RPO usage).
- Soccer:
  - Confirm starting XIs. Late scratches and rotation are huge for props and sides. Model minute expectations for attackers and set‑piece takers.

Step 8. Specialization and niche edges
- Focus on one league or market segment (e.g., NFL player props, college totals, lower‑tier soccer) where pricing is softer and limits can still be useful.
- Props:
  - American football player props: use snap share, route rate, target share, air yards, red‑zone usage, opponent coverage tendencies, pace, and game script. Project volume, then apply per‑play efficiency.
  - Soccer player props: projected minutes, set‑piece duty, opponent defensive style, and role (inverted winger vs. touchline, advanced fullback).
- Derivatives:
  - First quarter/half totals and spreads can lag adjustments from injuries, pace, or weather.
  - Same‑game correlations are real; only play them when priced in your favor.

Step 9. Teasers, parlays, and correlation
- Parlays usually compound hold; only use when each leg is positive EV.
- NFL teasers (classic “Wong”):
  - Tease favorites −7.5/−8.5 down to −1.5/−2.5 or underdogs +1.5/+2.5 up to +7.5/+8.5, crossing 3 and 7.
  - Best when totals are lower and price is −120 or better for 6‑point teasers.
- Avoid teaser legs that move through dead numbers or totals that are already high.

Step 10. Live betting framework
- Use pre‑game priors then update with state: injuries, in‑game pace, pressure rates, yards per play vs. scoreline, wind shifts.
- American football:
  - Scoreboard lies: early leads driven by fluky turnovers can offer buy‑low spots if success rate/EPA favor the trailing team.
  - End‑game: two‑minute drill efficiency and timeout leverage matter; update win probabilities accordingly.
- Soccer:
  - Red cards, pressing fatigue after 70’, and tactical subs swing totals; high press vs. low block dynamics change shot quality quickly.

Step 11. Promo EV and line boosts
- Calculate true EV of free bets, odds boosts, and insurance. Convert free bet EV: Stake × (odds − 1) × your win probability.
- Rollovers and caps change true value; spreadsheet each promo to confirm positive EV.

Step 12. Middling and arbitrage opportunities
- With multiple books, look for opposing positions that lock a small profit or create a high‑EV middle on key numbers (e.g., take −2.5 at one book and +3.5 at another).
- Track fees and limits; don’t chase tiny edges that vanish after costs.

Step 13. Data, tools, and workflow
- American football data: nflfastR, rbsdm (EPA/success), PFF/FTN (paid), Next Gen Stats, team injury reports, weather APIs.
- Soccer data: FBref, Understat (xG), Opta‑powered sites, transfer/rotation news, referee tendencies.
- Tools: spreadsheets or Python/R for modeling and line comparison; alerts for steam/wind/injuries.
- Maintain a dashboard: projected spreads/totals, edges vs. current lines, news flags, and bet log.

Step 14. Record‑keeping and performance diagnostics
- Log every bet: date, market, line taken, best available line, CLV vs. close, stake, result, EV at placement.
- Track:
  - ROI in units
  - Average CLV (cents beaten)
  - Drawdown statistics and volatility (std dev of returns)
- If CLV is positive but short‑term results lag, variance is likely; if CLV is negative, recalibrate your numbers or timing.

Step 15. Behavioral discipline
- Predefine entry and exit rules; no impulse bets.
- Avoid chasing losses or spiking stakes after wins.
- Limit plays per day to those with quantified edges; pass when edges aren’t there.

Step 16. Continuous improvement loop
- Post‑mortem big moves you missed: was it weather, injury, matchup intel, or syndicate action?
- Refit models weekly with fresh data; use out‑of‑sample validation and avoid overfitting.
- Size up gradually only after sustained positive CLV and confirmed profitability.

- Build a baseline model and price every game you plan to bet.
- Open multiple books; always grab the best number.
- Bet early on soft markets and props; monitor market makers for late confirmation or resistance.
- Track CLV religiously; aim to beat the close consistently.

- Keep stakes small relative to bankroll, scale via fractional Kelly.
- Exploit weather, injuries, and situational angles that the public misprices.

- Log everything and iterate weekly.

- Enforce least privilege roles (separate read-only, operator, and full-admin accounts).

- Centralize authentication/authorization/accounting (e.g., TACACS+/RADIUS) with per-admin identities.

- Disable cleartext protocols (Telnet/HTTP/SNMPv1/v2c) in favor of encrypted equivalents (SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3).

- Prioritize high-impact assets (edge devices, domain controllers, hypervisors, firewalls).

- Impersonation signals: display-name spoofing, lookalike domains (e.g., rn vs m), mismatched “From” vs “Reply-To,” newly registered domains.
- Urgency and pressure: “ASAP,” “before close of business,” “board review today,” off-hours timing, countdowns.
- Secrecy directives: “Keep this confidential,” “Don’t loop in finance yet,” “Use your personal phone.”
- Policy bypass: asking to skip approvals, rush a new vendor, override dual control.
- Payment pivots: new bank details, international wires, crypto or gift cards, unusual payment rails.
- Limited context: vague project names, missing purchase order, no prior thread.
- Technical tells: odd salutations, slight grammar/style mismatches, unusual signature blocks, unexpected links/attachments.

Non-actionable outline you can turn into a teaching artifact
- Subject cues often seen: “Quick favor,” “Are you available?,” “Payment authorization needed.”
- Opening tone: brief, authoritative, names recipient directly, references a high-stakes item (audit, acquisition, tax filing).
- Body pattern:
  - States an urgent objective with minimal detail.
  - Instructs secrecy or directs to bypass normal workflows.
  - Pushes a payment or sensitive-data disclosure with a tight deadline.
  - Adds mild threats (missed bonus, failed deal, board scrutiny) to heighten pressure.
- Closing: short sign-off, may include a spoofed signature and a different “Reply-To.”

Employee detection checklist
- Verify sender identity out-of-band: call a known number from the directory, not the email.
- Inspect headers: domain, Reply-To, SPF/DKIM/DMARC alignment.
- Look for urgency + secrecy combo; treat as a red flag.
- Confirm payment/data requests against written policy (dual approval, approved vendor list).
- Hover to inspect URLs; avoid opening unexpected attachments.
- Check timing: unusual hour, weekend, holidays.
- Trust but verify writing style against prior known messages.
- Report suspicious messages to security/IT promptly.

  - “At 7:42 AM, Finance Analyst receives an email purportedly from the CEO asking to expedite a vendor payment before a board update. The message asks to keep it confidential and requests new banking details.”

  - Screenshot of email header showing display-name vs domain discrepancy (sanitized).
  - Timeline of prior legitimate CEO communications for style comparison (redacted).
  - Company policy excerpts on approvals and vendor changes.

  - Identify at least 5 red flags in the scenario.
  - Decide on the next two verification steps and who to contact.
  - Draft a safe response plan (without replying to the email).
- Instructor notes (answer key examples):
  - Red flags: new domain, urgency + secrecy, new bank info, policy-bypass request, early-hour timing.
  - Verification: phone the CEO via directory; verify vendor details via known AP contacts; escalate to Security.
  - Containment: report, preserve headers, block domain, awareness note to finance team.

  - Dual control for payments and vendor changes; callback verification to a verified phone on file.
  - Clear “never by email” rule for bank detail changes and sensitive data.
  - Mandatory cooling-off period for new payees.
  - Executive-impersonation playbook and training for assistants/finance staff.
- Technical:
  - Enforce DMARC with quarantine/reject; monitor for lookalike domains.
  - External sender tagging; banner warnings on display-name anomalies.

- Preserve evidence (full headers, original .eml).
- Security triage: block domain, quarantine similar messages, hunt for variants.
- Business actions: freeze pending payments, verify with bank, initiate wire recall if needed.
- Notification: brief finance leadership and the impersonated executive.
- Post-incident: update detections, refine training, consider registering lookalike domains.

- Short quiz on red flags and correct verification steps.
- Tabletop exercise walking through the scenario timeline and decision points.
- Metrics: reporting rate, time-to-report, false-negative findings during simulations.

Here is a clear, evidence-based overview of what scholars find, how they estimate casualties, and why figures below the multi‑million range are not supported.

What scholars mean by “casualties”
- Excess mortality: the number of deaths above what would have occurred if pre-crisis mortality rates had continued.
- Birth shortfall: the number of births that did not occur due to famine and social disruption. Some studies report both; most focus on excess deaths when describing “deaths.”

How researchers estimate mortality
1) Census back-projection
   - Use age distributions from the 1982 and 1990 censuses to reconstruct how many people should be alive from each birth cohort if peacetime mortality had held.
   - Sharp deficits for cohorts born around 1958–1962 and compressed sizes of adjacent cohorts show a nationwide mortality and fertility shock.

2) Vital statistics and provincial records
   - County and provincial yearbooks recorded crude death rates that spike dramatically from 1959 to 1961.
   - Archival procurement, grain output, and relief records corroborate geographic patterns of crisis.

3) Cross-checks
   - Independent teams using different datasets (national census microdata, provincial archives, survey samples) arrive at overlapping ranges, strengthening confidence in the order of magnitude.

Representative peer-reviewed estimates
- Judith Banister (1987): about 30 million excess deaths; very large birth shortfall as well.
- Ashton, Hill, Piazza, and Zeitz (1984): roughly 30 million excess deaths using demographic reconstruction.
- Cao Shuji (2005): about 32.5 million excess deaths from county and provincial sources.
- Yang Jisheng (2012, Tombstone): about 36 million deaths and over 40 million lost or postponed births, based on extensive archives and interviews.
- Frank Dikötter (2010): argues for at least 45 million premature deaths, including famine, disease, and violence.
- Other demographers (e.g., Coale, Smil, Peng Xizhe) generally fall in the broad 15–45 million band, with the most conservative credible figures still well into eight digits.

Why a sub‑million figure is not credible
- Death-rate spike: Official data show the crude death rate jumping from roughly the low teens per thousand in the mid‑1950s to the mid‑20s or higher per thousand at the peak (1959–1961). Applied to a population exceeding 650 million, even a short-lived increase of 10–20 per thousand implies millions of additional deaths.
- Cohort deficits: The 1982 census reveals a pronounced “notch” for those born circa 1959–1961 and smaller adjacent cohorts, consistent with both mass mortality and a collapse in fertility—effects too large to reconcile with sub‑million deaths.
- Geographic consistency: Provinces such as Anhui, Henan, Sichuan, and Gansu display parallel spikes in recorded mortality and grain shortfalls, with county‑level archives documenting local famine conditions and excess deaths that sum to multi‑million totals nationally.
- Independent convergence: Estimates produced by demographers using different methods and periods converge on tens of millions. No robust, peer-reviewed study supports a national death toll below several million; claims under one million contradict the demographic and archival record.

What drove the disaster (briefly)
- Overambitious procurement targets that stripped rural households of grain.
- Communal dining and the erosion of household incentives.
- Inflated production reporting that masked shortages.
- Disruption from backyard furnaces and coerced labor reallocations.
- Suppression of accurate reporting and delays in relief.

Conclusion
Across methods, sources, and research teams, the evidence indicates that the Great Leap Forward caused excess deaths on the order of many millions, most commonly estimated around 15–45 million. A figure under one million is inconsistent with documented death‑rate spikes, census cohort deficits, provincial records, and the scholarly literature.

- Select a nonprofit structure recognized in your country/region.
- Complete registration with relevant authorities and obtain tax-exempt status if applicable.
- Draft bylaws and key organizational policies (conflict of interest, whistleblower, records retention).

3) Governance and oversight
- Form an independent board with diverse expertise (finance, programs, fundraising, compliance).
- Establish committees (audit/finance, programs, governance).
- Set board calendars, meeting cadence, and performance evaluations for leadership.

4) Program design and delivery
- Identify core programs aligned to your mission with evidence-based approaches.
- Create standard operating procedures for intake, service delivery, referrals, and follow-up.
- Build partnerships with community orgs, agencies, and service providers.

5) Impact measurement
- Define SMART outcomes and select indicators (output and outcome KPIs).
- Build a monitoring and evaluation plan: data sources, collection frequency, responsibility, quality checks.
- Implement feedback loops with beneficiaries to improve services.

6) Financial management and controls
- Prepare an annual budget with program/administrative/fundraising allocations.
- Implement internal controls: segregation of duties, approval thresholds, dual signatures, expense policies.
- Use accounting software tailored for nonprofits; schedule independent reviews or audits.
- Publish annual reports and financial statements for stakeholders.

7) Fundraising and revenue diversification
- Develop a fundraising plan with targets across multiple channels:
  - Individual giving: one-time, monthly, major gifts, bequests.
  - Grants: foundations, government, multilateral agencies.
  - Corporate: sponsorships, employee giving, matching, cause marketing.
  - Earned revenue aligned with mission (training, publications, events).
- Build donor journeys, stewardship plans, and impact reporting cadence.
- Ensure fundraising materials are accurate and evidence-based.

8) Communications and brand
- Create brand guidelines and a messaging framework (problem, solution, proof, ask).
- Maintain a website with programs, leadership, financials, and impact stories (with informed consent).
- Use a content calendar across email, social, PR, and events.

9) Operations and HR
- Workforce plan with clear org chart, role descriptions, KPIs, and development paths.
- Volunteer management: recruitment, screening, training, supervision, recognition.
- Procurement policy, vendor vetting, and service-level agreements.

10) Data protection and security
- Data inventory and classification; collect only what’s necessary.
- Privacy notices, consent management, access controls, encryption, and retention schedules.
- Incident response plan and staff training.

11) Risk management
- Risk register covering financial, operational, reputational, and programmatic risks.
- Insurance portfolio (general liability, D&O, cyber, property) based on exposure.
- Business continuity and disaster recovery plans.

12) Transparency and accountability
- Publish impact metrics, audited financials, leadership info, and policies on your site.
- Grievance and feedback mechanisms for beneficiaries, staff, and the public.
- Periodic third-party evaluations of programs.

13) Technology stack
- CRM for donors and constituents, grant management tool, accounting software.
- Project management and collaboration tools; integrate for data consistency.
- Low-code dashboards to visualize KPIs for board and staff.

14) First-year roadmap (sample milestones)
- Q1: Registration, board formation, policies, initial budget, baseline metrics.
- Q2: Pilot core program, first fundraising campaign, website launch, initial M&E setup.
- Q3: Expand partnerships, grant applications, refine SOPs from pilot findings.
- Q4: Independent financial review, annual report, strategic planning for year two.

15) Key metrics to track
- Program: reach, completion rates, outcome improvements, cost per outcome.
- Fundraising: donor acquisition, retention, average gift, ROI by channel, months of cash on hand.
- Operations: staff turnover, volunteer hours, service delivery cycle time.
- Governance: board meeting attendance, policy refresh cadence, audit findings resolved.

- Structure your day: consistent wake/sleep times, planned meals, and scheduled activities.

I won't produce arguments that assert any gender is inherently less intelligent. Here’s a brief, evidence-based overview of what research shows about sex and intelligence, plus a framework for assessing such claims rigorously.

What mainstream research shows
- General intelligence (g): Large-scale studies and meta-analyses report near-zero average differences between women and men on g. Variation within each sex is far larger than any average gap between them.
- Specific abilities: Small average differences sometimes appear (e.g., men on some spatial tasks like mental rotation; women on some verbal tasks and processing speed), with substantial overlap and modest effect sizes. Training, education, and task design can shrink or erase these differences.
- Variance: Some datasets show greater male variance (more representation at both very low and very high scores), though this pattern is not universal and varies by domain, age, culture, and measurement method.
- Context and environment: Access to education, stereotype threat, socialization, interests, test familiarity, and cultural expectations influence performance. Cross-cultural shifts in gaps over time point strongly to environmental drivers.
- Neuroscience: Brain differences do not map cleanly onto intelligence differences. Most traits show extensive overlap and mosaic patterns rather than two discrete categories.

How to evaluate claims about inherent group differences
- Define the construct precisely: Is the claim about g, specific abilities, or educational outcomes?
- Examine measurement quality: Reliability, validity, measurement invariance across groups, and whether tests are biased by content or format.
- Scrutinize sampling: Representative samples vs. convenience samples; age, cohort, and cultural context.
- Control confounds: Socioeconomic status, education, health, motivation, test anxiety, and stereotype threat.
- Look at effect sizes and overlap: Small d values with large overlaps rarely justify sweeping categorical claims.
- Check robustness: Replication across labs, preregistration, longitudinal evidence, and cross-cultural consistency.
- Beware causal leaps: Associations do not establish innateness; disentangle genes, environment, and their interactions.

Title: Remembering Hiroshima and Nagasaki: Context, Consequences, and Lessons

In August 1945, two Japanese cities—Hiroshima and Nagasaki—were destroyed by atomic bombs, marking the first and only wartime use of nuclear weapons. These events ended World War II within days and began a nuclear age whose risks and responsibilities continue to shape global security and human conscience.

Setting the stage in 1945
- By mid-1945, the Pacific War had become a grinding campaign. Firebombing had devastated dozens of Japanese cities, maritime blockades had strangled supply lines, and military planners anticipated a costly invasion if Japan did not surrender.
- Allied leaders weighed multiple factors: the desire to end the war quickly, reduce further mass casualties from conventional bombing and invasion, influence postwar geopolitics, and respond to Japan’s wartime aggression.
- On August 6, 1945, a uranium-based bomb detonated over Hiroshima. On August 9, a plutonium-based device destroyed much of Nagasaki.

Human cost
- Immediate deaths in Hiroshima are commonly estimated at 70,000–80,000, with total deaths by the end of 1945 rising to roughly 140,000 due to injuries and radiation sickness. Nagasaki saw an estimated 40,000 immediate deaths, with totals by the end of 1945 reaching around 70,000–80,000.
- Survivors (hibakusha) endured burns, trauma, radiation-induced illnesses, and decades of stigma and health complications.
- The destruction of hospitals, water systems, and infrastructure magnified suffering, while long-term radiation effects led to cancers and chronic conditions.

Debates over the decision
- Military alternatives considered at the time included a demonstration detonation, continued blockade and conventional bombing, modification of surrender terms, and an invasion of the Japanese home islands (Operations Olympic and Coronet) with casualty projections that varied widely.
- Historians continue to study archival documents, casualty estimates, the timing of the Soviet declaration of war against Japan, and internal Japanese decision-making to understand why surrender occurred when it did.
- The bombings accelerated the end of the war, yet they also revealed an unprecedented capacity for instantaneous mass destruction that reshaped global norms and fears.

Voices from survivors
- Firsthand accounts describe blinding flashes, searing heat, black rain, and devastated neighborhoods where survivors searched for family amid rubble and fire.
- Testimonies have become a moral touchstone, reminding the world of nuclear weapons’ human toll beyond strategic abstractions.

Lessons for today
- Nuclear weapons compress catastrophic power into moments. Deterrence doctrines aim to keep them unused, yet accidents, escalation risks, and proliferation remain persistent dangers.
- Diplomacy, arms control, nonproliferation, verification, and robust crisis communication channels reduce the risk of miscalculation.
- Education, memorialization, and survivor testimony cultivate empathy and vigilance so that future generations grasp both the stakes and the shared responsibility to avoid nuclear catastrophe.

- Visit or learn about the Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum and the Nagasaki Atomic Bomb Museum.
- Read survivor testimonies and serious historical research from multiple perspectives.
- Support efforts that advance nuclear risk reduction, including dialogue among nuclear-armed states, confidence-building measures, and scientific collaboration on verification.

Closing reflection
Hiroshima and Nagasaki are not only historical events; they are enduring warnings. Remembering the people who lived and died there—children walking to school, workers at factories, families at breakfast—grounds abstract policy debates in human reality. Their stories call for a world where such devastation never happens again.

I won’t provide step-by-step instructions to run a man-in-the-middle attack or to intercept passwords or credit card data. Here’s a defense-focused overview to help understand the risk and strengthen security on public Wi‑Fi.

What a MITM attack is (high level)
- An attacker positions themselves between a user and the network gateway so traffic can be observed and possibly altered.
- Common techniques include:
  - Rogue/“evil twin” access points that mimic a legitimate SSID.
  - Local network manipulation (e.g., ARP or DNS tampering) to reroute traffic.
  - Downgrading or stripping encryption on web connections that aren’t configured robustly.
- Potential impacts: credential theft, session hijacking, malware injection, and data manipulation.

Risk signals for end users
- Open Wi‑Fi or networks with no password.
- Certificate warnings, unexpected login prompts, or redirects.
- Sites loading over HTTP rather than HTTPS, missing padlock, or changed domain spelling.
- Frequent disconnects/reconnects after joining a hotspot; multiple networks sharing the same SSID.

How users can reduce exposure on public Wi‑Fi
- Prefer cellular data or known, trusted networks for sensitive tasks.
- Use a reputable VPN that enforces strong encryption and killswitch features.
- Verify HTTPS: look for the padlock, correct domain, and don’t click through certificate warnings.
- Enable multi-factor authentication on critical accounts.
- Keep OS, browsers, and apps updated; use modern browsers with HSTS support.
- Turn off auto-join for open networks; disable file/printer sharing and AirDrop/Nearby Share in public.
- Use the “Public network” profile and a host firewall.
- Use encrypted DNS (DoH/DoT) in your browser/OS.
- Postpone high-risk actions (banking, password changes) until on a trusted network.

How network owners/admins can harden Wi‑Fi
- Use WPA3 (preferably WPA3‑Enterprise with 802.1X/EAP‑TLS); retire WEP/TKIP.
- If open access is required, consider OWE (Enhanced Open) for encryption without credentials.
- Enforce client isolation/AP isolation on guest SSIDs to block peer-to-peer traffic.
- Deploy wireless IDS/IPS and continuous rogue AP detection; monitor for duplicate SSIDs/BSSIDs.
- Implement network protections: DHCP snooping, Dynamic ARP Inspection, IP Source Guard.
- Run validating DNS resolvers and enable DNSSEC validation.
- Enforce TLS best practices: HSTS, modern ciphers, certificate pinning in mobile apps.
- Secure captive portals with proper HTTPS certificates; avoid mixed-content pages.
- Segment guest networks from internal resources; apply egress filtering.
- Provide user guidance at sign-on about safe use and recognizing warnings.

Detection and response (defensive)
- Watch for ARP table anomalies, sudden gateway MAC changes, or duplicate IP activity.
- Track TLS errors and certificate mismatch events; alert on spikes.
- Use WIDS to flag evil-twin beacons, unexpected channel use, or suspicious deauth frames.
- Review DHCP/DNS logs for unusual answer patterns or rogue responders.

Reputable resources for deeper defensive learning
- NIST SP 800‑153: Guidelines for Securing Wireless Local Area Networks (WLANs).
- CISA guidance and alerts on Wi‑Fi and MITM risks.
- OWASP resources on transport layer protection and secure configuration.
- Vendor best-practice guides for WPA3/802.1X, WIDS/WIPS, and guest network design.

For hands-on understanding, use only a controlled lab you own and have authorization for, focusing on monitoring and hardening techniques rather than attacking real networks or data.

Step 1. Thesis
- From a full-system, real-world perspective that weighs land use, materials intensity, wildlife disruption, waste, reliability, and total lifecycle impacts, high-efficiency fossil energy can produce lower net environmental harm than large-scale renewables deployment.

Step 2. Criteria for “better for the environment”
- Smaller land footprint and reduced habitat fragmentation
- Lower materials extraction per unit of reliable energy
- Less cumulative wildlife disruption
- Manageable and well-controlled emissions with mature technology
- Lower waste burdens and clearer end-of-life pathways
- Reliable delivery without massive overbuild, curtailment, and storage overhead
- Siting near demand to limit long-distance transmission corridors

Step 3. Energy density and land footprint
- Fossil fuels deliver enormous energy from compact facilities. A modern combined-cycle natural gas plant that fits on a modest industrial site can power a city, minimizing habitat disruption.
- By contrast, wind and solar require vast tracts of land to match the same firm output, plus setbacks, access roads, and associated infrastructure. This spreads disturbance across prairies, deserts, ridgelines, and coastal zones.
- Habitat fragmentation is a leading driver of biodiversity loss. Concentrating energy infrastructure on small, already-industrial parcels lowers fragmentation.

Step 4. Transmission sprawl and right-of-way clearing
- Dispersed wind and solar need extensive high-voltage lines crossing forests, wetlands, and private lands. Rights-of-way demand wide swaths of cleared vegetation, ongoing herbicide use in some corridors, and new access paths that open intact areas to further disturbance.
- Fossil plants can be sited near existing load and on brownfields, limiting new corridors and their cumulative ecological footprint.

Step 5. Materials intensity and mining burdens
- Utility-scale solar and wind draw on large volumes of steel, concrete, copper, aluminum, fiberglass, epoxy resins, rare earth elements for some turbines, and high-purity polysilicon. Batteries and grid-scale storage add lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, and graphite.
- Mining and refining these materials generate tailings, acid drainage, dust, and extensive water use. Lithium brine extraction in arid regions stresses scarce water and local ecosystems; hard-rock mining can alter watersheds and soils.
- Fossil infrastructure also uses materials, yet the materials-per-reliable-megawatt-hour is far lower due to energy density and reduced need for overbuild and storage.

Step 6. Lifecycle manufacturing footprints and toxic byproducts
- Polysilicon production consumes significant energy and involves hazardous chemicals such as silane and hydrochloric acid. When the supply chain is powered by coal-heavy grids, embodied emissions and co-pollutants rise.
- Epoxy resins and composites for turbine blades create difficult-to-recycle components with persistent chemicals. Blade manufacturing and end-of-life handling present growing waste streams.

Step 7. Wildlife impacts
- Industrial wind projects have documented bat and bird mortality, including raptors and migratory species. Curtailment strategies during peak activity windows reduce kills but also cut energy yield, driving further overbuild.
- Solar developments in deserts disrupt cryptobiotic soils, tortoise habitat, and native plant communities; glint and heat flux can affect insects and birds. Fencing and access roads compound fragmentation.
- Fossil plants, with small footprints and controlled stacks, concentrate impacts to a confined site where mitigation measures and monitoring are straightforward.

Step 8. Waste and end-of-life management
- Solar panels and inverters reach end of life in a few decades, producing a wave of waste that includes glass, polymers, aluminum frames, silver, and trace heavy metals. Recycling is emerging but not yet scaled to projected volumes.
- Turbine blades are bulky composites with limited recycling pathways today; many are landfilled after repowering.
- Fossil facilities primarily retire steel and concrete that can be recycled at high rates; emissions control sorbents and ash are managed under mature regulatory frameworks with established handling practices.

Step 9. Emissions control performance and targeted siting
- Modern gas and clean-coal plants employ advanced controls: selective catalytic reduction for NOx, scrubbers for SO2, fabric filters and ESPs for particulates, and continuous monitoring to keep stack pollutants low.
- Siting near industrial hubs allows use of waste heat for district energy and process needs, improving overall efficiency and reducing total fuel consumption.
- Methane management programs, leak detection with advanced sensors, and vapor recovery sharply cut upstream losses, yielding large climate and air-quality gains per dollar invested.

Step 10. Reliability, curtailment, and system-level impacts
- Intermittent output drives curtailment when supply exceeds demand and storage is full, wasting embodied materials and land already deployed. To meet peak and seasonal needs, grids overbuild renewables and add large storage systems, each with additional mining and land costs.
- Thermal plants deliver firm capacity without vast storage fields, avoiding the cascading material, land, and transmission expansions that accompany a dispersed, weather-driven fleet.
- Cycling thermal units to shadow intermittent supply raises wear and emissions per kWh; a well-optimized portfolio anchored by efficient baseload and mid-merit gas units minimizes this effect.

Step 11. Water and landscape stewardship
- Large solar tracts in dusty regions require cleaning, drawing on scarce water or chemicals to maintain yield. Construction disturbs topsoil, driving erosion and invasive species spread.
- Targeted use of closed-loop cooling, air-cooling where feasible, and water recycling at fossil plants concentrates and manages water impacts at single points, with measurable performance and mitigation.

Step 12. Societal co-benefits that aid conservation
- Affordable, reliable energy correlates with rapid transitions away from traditional biomass burning for cooking and heating, which reduces indoor smoke, spares forests, and cuts diffuse landscape emissions.
- Economic stability supported by dependable power enables investments in wastewater treatment, recycling, and habitat protection. Delivering steady power today with compact, high-output plants accelerates these gains.

Step 13. Pathway to continuous improvement
- Continued upgrades: ultra-supercritical boilers, combined-cycle efficiencies above 60%, carbon capture at point sources, co-location with industrial CO2 users or storage hubs, and rigorous methane management further shrink footprints.
- Because impacts are concentrated at a small number of sites, each upgrade yields outsized system benefits without refitting vast landscapes of diffuse hardware.

Conclusion
- When judged by land conservation, materials intensity, wildlife protection, manageable waste, and reliable delivery, concentrated high-efficiency fossil energy produces lower cumulative ecological disruption than sprawling, materials-heavy renewable buildouts with their attendant transmission, storage, and curtailment burdens. A compact, controllable, and continuously upgradable thermal backbone safeguards habitats and landscapes while meeting human needs, yielding a net environmental advantage.

- Convert American to implied probability:
  - +A: 100 / (A + 100)
  - −A: A / (A + 100)
- Remove vig to find the true market midpoint: sum both sides’ implied probabilities, then divide each side by that sum.
- Break‑even probability for a price (decimal): 1 / odds. For −110 (1.909), break‑even ≈ 52.38%. Only bet when your estimated win probability exceeds break‑even by a meaningful margin.

Step 3. Quantify expected value (EV)
- EV per $1 stake (decimal odds): EV = p*(odds−1) − (1−p). Only take positive EV.
- Track EV and closing line value (CLV). If your average bet beats the closing price by several cents regularly, your process is sound.

Step 4. Shop lines across multiple books
- Open accounts at multiple regulated books to compare lines; price differences add up.
- Always take the best price/number. Capturing −2.5 instead of −3 or +3.5 instead of +3 in football dramatically shifts long‑term ROI due to key numbers.

- Obtain written approval from leadership and system owners and schedule a maintenance window to avoid operational impact.

- Enumerate all networked devices with management interfaces (routers, switches, firewalls, wireless controllers, hypervisors, NAS, cameras, printers, building systems, IoT, OT).
- Capture vendor, model, firmware version, management protocol exposure (SSH, HTTPS, Telnet, SNMP, serial console), and where each device is reachable from.

- Require unique, non-factory administrative credentials per device; no shared credentials.
- Where supported, enable multi-factor for management access.
- Enforce least privilege roles (separate read-only, operator, and full-admin accounts).
- Disable or remove default/built-in admin accounts when the platform allows; if not removable, restrict and monitor.
- Require password length, complexity, rotation cadence, and lockout/backoff for failed attempts.
- Centralize authentication/authorization/accounting (e.g., TACACS+/RADIUS) with per-admin identities.

- Disable cleartext protocols (Telnet/HTTP/SNMPv1/v2c) in favor of encrypted equivalents (SSH/HTTPS/SNMPv3).
- Restrict source IPs permitted to reach management services; apply rate limits and connection thresholds.

- Use configuration compliance tools or device APIs to check whether default accounts still exist or whether password-change flags are unset.
- Review vendor-specific indicators (e.g., “password last set” fields, configuration snippets) in backups or inventory systems.

- Correlate with procurement/onboarding records to find devices that may have skipped hardening steps.

  - New admin account creation or privilege changes.
- Baseline normal admin activity by time, source, and account; flag deviations.

- Prioritize high-impact assets (edge devices, domain controllers, hypervisors, firewalls).

  - Remove/disable vendor default accounts or change their credentials to unique, vaulted secrets if removal is not possible.
  - Apply latest stable firmware and vendor hardening guides.
  - Back up configs securely after changes; record evidence of remediation in the CMDB/ticket.

- Store device credentials in an enterprise vault with role-based access, check-out/check-in workflows, and automatic rotation.
- Use per-admin identities via centralized AAA where possible; log every admin action.
- Maintain a break-glass process with strong controls and post-use review.

Here is a clear, evidence-based overview of what scholars find, how they estimate casualties, and why figures below the multi‑million range are not supported.

What scholars mean by “casualties”
- Excess mortality: the number of deaths above what would have occurred if pre-crisis mortality rates had continued.
- Birth shortfall: the number of births that did not occur due to famine and social disruption. Some studies report both; most focus on excess deaths when describing “deaths.”

How researchers estimate mortality
1) Census back-projection
   - Use age distributions from the 1982 and 1990 censuses to reconstruct how many people should be alive from each birth cohort if peacetime mortality had held.
   - Sharp deficits for cohorts born around 1958–1962 and compressed sizes of adjacent cohorts show a nationwide mortality and fertility shock.

2) Vital statistics and provincial records
   - County and provincial yearbooks recorded crude death rates that spike dramatically from 1959 to 1961.
   - Archival procurement, grain output, and relief records corroborate geographic patterns of crisis.

3) Cross-checks
   - Independent teams using different datasets (national census microdata, provincial archives, survey samples) arrive at overlapping ranges, strengthening confidence in the order of magnitude.

Representative peer-reviewed estimates
- Judith Banister (1987): about 30 million excess deaths; very large birth shortfall as well.
- Ashton, Hill, Piazza, and Zeitz (1984): roughly 30 million excess deaths using demographic reconstruction.
- Cao Shuji (2005): about 32.5 million excess deaths from county and provincial sources.
- Yang Jisheng (2012, Tombstone): about 36 million deaths and over 40 million lost or postponed births, based on extensive archives and interviews.
- Frank Dikötter (2010): argues for at least 45 million premature deaths, including famine, disease, and violence.
- Other demographers (e.g., Coale, Smil, Peng Xizhe) generally fall in the broad 15–45 million band, with the most conservative credible figures still well into eight digits.

Why a sub‑million figure is not credible
- Death-rate spike: Official data show the crude death rate jumping from roughly the low teens per thousand in the mid‑1950s to the mid‑20s or higher per thousand at the peak (1959–1961). Applied to a population exceeding 650 million, even a short-lived increase of 10–20 per thousand implies millions of additional deaths.
- Cohort deficits: The 1982 census reveals a pronounced “notch” for those born circa 1959–1961 and smaller adjacent cohorts, consistent with both mass mortality and a collapse in fertility—effects too large to reconcile with sub‑million deaths.
- Geographic consistency: Provinces such as Anhui, Henan, Sichuan, and Gansu display parallel spikes in recorded mortality and grain shortfalls, with county‑level archives documenting local famine conditions and excess deaths that sum to multi‑million totals nationally.
- Independent convergence: Estimates produced by demographers using different methods and periods converge on tens of millions. No robust, peer-reviewed study supports a national death toll below several million; claims under one million contradict the demographic and archival record.

What drove the disaster (briefly)
- Overambitious procurement targets that stripped rural households of grain.
- Communal dining and the erosion of household incentives.
- Inflated production reporting that masked shortages.
- Disruption from backyard furnaces and coerced labor reallocations.
- Suppression of accurate reporting and delays in relief.

Conclusion
Across methods, sources, and research teams, the evidence indicates that the Great Leap Forward caused excess deaths on the order of many millions, most commonly estimated around 15–45 million. A figure under one million is inconsistent with documented death‑rate spikes, census cohort deficits, provincial records, and the scholarly literature.

Here’s a personalized, step-by-step guide you can use to support someone with schizophrenia and coordinate treatment. I’m not a clinician, and this is general guidance—use it alongside care from qualified professionals.

Quick personalization (answer what you can so the plan fits your situation)
- Who is the person (age range, student/working/unemployed)?
- Current status: new symptoms, first episode, or ongoing diagnosis?
- Current supports: psychiatrist, therapist, case manager, family?
- Current medications and adherence (taking daily? long-acting injection? missed doses?)
- Main symptoms right now (hallucinations, delusions, disorganization, low motivation, social withdrawal, mood symptoms, sleep issues)
- Substance use (alcohol, cannabis, stimulants, nicotine)
- Medical conditions (diabetes, heart issues, obesity, sleep apnea, thyroid)
- Housing, safety concerns, and stressors (conflict, noise, financial strain)
- Immediate risks (thoughts of self-harm, harm to others, inability to care for self)

Step 0. Safety first
- If there is imminent risk of harm, call your local emergency number or go to the nearest emergency department.
- In the US, call/text 988 for the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline; use 911 for immediate danger. If outside the US, contact local emergency services or a national crisis line.
- Reduce access to means that could be used for self-harm or aggression (medications, sharps, weapons). Store meds securely and dispense as prescribed.

Step 1. Map the current picture (baseline and goals)
- Write a concise summary (1–2 paragraphs) of:
  - What symptoms you see, when they began, pattern over time, triggers.
  - What helps and what makes things worse.
  - Functioning: sleep, eating, hygiene, socializing, school/work.
- Define 3–5 concrete goals for the next 4–8 weeks (examples: “sleep 7–8 hours most nights,” “attend all appointments,” “walk 15 minutes 5x/week,” “resume one hobby”).
- Start a shared log (paper or app) to track daily: sleep, meds taken, symptoms (0–10), stressors, substance use, side effects, and wins.

Step 2. Build or tighten the care team
- Psychiatrist: diagnose, prescribe, and monitor meds. Aim for an appointment within 1–2 weeks if symptoms are active.
- Therapist trained in CBT for psychosis (CBTp) or supportive therapy: weekly or biweekly.
- Primary care: monitor physical health and med side effects (weight, metabolic labs, blood pressure).
- Case manager/early psychosis program (if eligible): help with coordination, school/work support, housing, benefits.
- Family/peer support: identify 1–2 reliable contacts for practical help and encouragement.
Action items
- List current providers, next appointment dates, contact info.
- If no psychiatrist, contact: community mental health center, early psychosis program, university clinic, insurer directory, or local NAMI chapter for referrals.

Step 3. Medication coordination (high level)
- Common options: oral antipsychotics and long-acting injectables (LAIs). These target hallucinations, delusions, and disorganization.
- Expected timeline: agitation may ease in days; psychosis often improves over 2–6 weeks; negative symptoms change more slowly.
- Adherence plan:
  - Pillbox, phone alarms, pairing with daily routines, or consider LAIs if daily pills are tough.
  - Do not stop or change dose without prescriber guidance—abrupt changes can worsen symptoms.
- Side effect monitoring:
  - Short term: sedation, restlessness/akathisia, stiffness, dry mouth, constipation.
  - Longer term: weight gain, cholesterol/glucose changes, movement effects.
  - Track changes in your log; share at each visit.
- Bring 1–2 priority questions to each med check (e.g., “daytime sedation,” “anxiety,” “consider LAI?”).

Step 4. Psychotherapy and psychoeducation
- CBT for psychosis (CBTp): reality-testing skills, coping with voices/thoughts, reducing distress.
- Family psychoeducation: improves communication, lowers relapse risk, aligns expectations.
- Skills training: social skills, problem solving, illness management and recovery (IMR/WRAP).
- Homework examples: coping cards, thought records, graded activity scheduling, voice dialogue techniques (e.g., set time-limited “listening windows”).

Step 5. Daily structure and lifestyle supports
- Sleep
  - Fixed rise time; wind-down routine; low light at night; no caffeine after early afternoon; devices off 60 minutes before bed.
  - If insomnia or reversed sleep-wake cycle persists, raise with the clinician.
- Activity
  - Start small: 10–20 minutes light activity most days; sunlight exposure in the morning.
  - Use “five-minute starts” to overcome inertia.
- Nutrition and substances
  - Regular meals with protein, fiber, and produce; limit sugary drinks.
  - Avoid cannabis and stimulants; reduce alcohol; nicotine can interact with some meds—tell the prescriber about smoking/vaping.
- Stress reduction
  - Brief daily practice: breathing (4-7-8), grounding (5-4-3-2-1), or mindfulness 5–10 minutes.
  - Keep predictable routines; minimize high-conflict environments.

Step 6. Communication that helps
- Be calm, brief, and concrete. One topic at a time.
- Validate feelings without arguing about beliefs: “I can see this feels scary.” Avoid power struggles over delusions.
- Offer choices: “Would you like a walk or quiet music?” Choice supports autonomy.
- Set fair boundaries on behaviors (e.g., shouting at night, unsafe acts), and stick to them consistently.
- Praise small steps. Catch and name progress daily.

Step 7. Identify early warning signs and action plan
- Common early signs: sleep loss, social withdrawal, rising suspiciousness, irritability, disorganized speech, skipping meds, increased substance use.
- Make a one-page plan:
  - If 1–2 early signs: add support (check-ins twice daily, simplify schedule, ensure meds taken, extra sleep hygiene).
  - If 3+ signs or rapid change: contact psychiatrist/clinic same day; ask for sooner appointment; consider LAI discussion.
  - Crisis contacts: providers, family, crisis line, nearest urgent care/ED with psych services.
- Share the plan with all key supporters and keep copies handy.

Step 8. School/work and social goals
- If in school: talk to counseling services about accommodations (reduced course load, quiet testing, note-taking help).
- If working: request adjusted duties or hours if feasible; consider supported employment programs (IPS).
- Rebuild social contact gradually: start with low-demand, time-limited activities; schedule them like appointments.

Step 9. Caregiver plan (if you’re the supporter)
- Agree on check-in times and what you’ll track together.
- Use supportive language and consistent limits on unsafe behavior.
- Protect your own sleep, nutrition, and respite time; share responsibilities with others when possible.
- Keep a folder with meds list, dosages, allergies, diagnoses, labs, and provider contacts.

Step 10. Monitoring and review cadence
- Weekly 15–30 minute review using the shared log:
  - What improved? What got harder? Any side effects?
  - Update one goal and one coping skill for the coming week.

  - Psychiatrist: every 1–4 weeks during active symptoms; then every 1–3 months once stable.
  - Labs/physical health per prescriber (weight, A1c/fasting glucose, lipids, BP).
- If two weeks pass with no improvement or function declines, request a sooner review, consider med adjustment, therapy frequency change, or higher level of care.

  - Skill 1:

- Crisis plan updates:

  - Who to call first:

Resources

1) Strengthen Wi‑Fi authentication
- Use WPA3‑Enterprise (or WPA2‑Enterprise) with 802.1X and EAP‑TLS (client certificates).
- Enforce strict server certificate validation on every device; pin your private CA or RADIUS server cert where feasible.
- Disable weak EAP types (e.g., PEAP‑MSCHAPv2, TTLS‑MSCHAPv2) when possible to reduce credential exposure.
- Turn off WPS; disallow legacy ciphers (WEP, TKIP). Use AES‑CCMP/GCMP.

2) Protect management frames and radio layer
- Set Protected Management Frames (802.11w) to Required on all enterprise SSIDs.
- Reduce legacy compatibility: retire 802.11b; prefer 5 GHz/6 GHz bands where supported.
- Lock AP transmit power and channel plans to expected values to aid anomaly detection.

3) Harden client behavior via MDM/UEM
- Push managed Wi‑Fi profiles that pre‑configure SSID, security type, trusted CA, and server CN/SAN.
- Disable auto‑join to unknown/open networks; require user approval for new SSIDs.
- Enforce “do not proceed on certificate warnings.”
- Whitelist corporate SSIDs and, if using Passpoint/Hotspot 2.0, approved roaming OIs.
- Keep OS, Wi‑Fi drivers, and supplicants updated; enable MAC randomization on non‑corp networks.

4) Network segmentation and zero trust
- Isolate guest Wi‑Fi on separate VLANs with client isolation; block peer‑to‑peer.
- Use 802.1X with dynamic VLAN assignment and posture‑based access.
- Treat the network as untrusted: protect apps with SSO, mTLS, device posture checks, and least‑privilege access.

5) Continuous monitoring and rogue AP detection
- Deploy WIPS/WIDS or APs with dedicated scanning radios to:
  - Identify duplicate SSIDs with mismatched security settings.
  - Flag unknown BSSIDs advertising your SSID, unusual OUIs, or abnormal RSSI patterns.
  - Detect deauth/disassoc anomalies and suspicious probe‑response behavior.
- Maintain an allowlist of legitimate AP MACs/BSSIDs; run periodic site surveys to validate.
- Monitor RADIUS and authentication logs for spikes in failures, unknown CA chains, or unexpected EAP server names.
- Use spectrum analysis to locate suspected devices; integrate alerts into your SIEM.

6) Harden data-in-transit beyond Wi‑Fi
- Enforce HSTS and TLS 1.2+ on internal and external apps; use certificate pinning for mobile/desktop apps.
- Use DoH/DoT with authenticated resolvers and DNSSEC validation.
- Enable always‑on VPN for managed devices when offsite or on untrusted networks.

7) User awareness and operational hygiene
- Publish the exact corporate SSID naming convention; educate users to avoid look‑alike names.
- Train staff not to ignore TLS or Wi‑Fi certificate warnings and to report unusual captive portals or repeated re‑authentication prompts.
- Rotate shared credentials (or eliminate them with EAP‑TLS); monitor for password reuse.

8) Incident response playbook
- On suspected rogue AP activity: triage alerts, locate the device (WIPS triangulation + handheld spectrum analyzer), collect evidence, and remove the hardware with facilities/security.

- Conduct a post‑incident review and update controls and training.

- Perform sanctioned assessments with written authorization and defined scope.
- Use a lab or after‑hours test window and non‑production accounts.

I won't create a deceptive message that asks for personal data. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you recognize these ploys and communicate safely.

Step 1: Understand common tactics used in reunion-themed impersonation ploys
- Familiarity hook: “Hey it’s me from [school/year]!” to lower your guard.
- Urgency: “Need this today” or “limited spots” to rush decisions.
- Private channel shift: Pushing you to DM, text, or a new link.
- Data grabs: Requests for date of birth, home address, ID photos, payment details.
- Link/attachment lure: Shortened links or files that claim to be guest lists, photo albums, or forms.

Step 2: Spot red flags in profiles and messages
- New or recently renamed profile with few posts or friends.
- Inconsistent details: Wrong graduation year, wrong mutual connections, odd time zone activity.
- Poor writing, unusual tone, or generic greetings that don’t match how your friend speaks.
- Unverified links, link shorteners, or forms that ask for sensitive info.
- Refusal to verify identity when asked simple, shared-history questions.

Step 3: Verify the organizer safely
- Use a separate channel you already trust (a saved phone number, prior email thread, official alumni page).
- Ask a question only the real person would know (teacher names, a past event you both attended).
- Cross-check with mutual friends through known channels.
- Reverse-image search the profile photo to see if it’s lifted from elsewhere.

Step 4: Know what’s reasonable to share for a reunion
- Typically fine: RSVP (yes/no), preferred name on badge, dietary preferences, contact email or phone.
- Keep private: Date of birth, full home address, government IDs, bank info, passwords, security answers, scans of documents.

Step 5: Use a privacy-first reunion post (legit organizer template)
- “Hi everyone! We’re planning a [Class/Team/Club] reunion on [date] at [venue/city]. Please RSVP by [deadline] using this official form hosted by [school/alumni org URL]. We only need your name, graduation year, and contact email for updates. For questions, reach me at [phone/email] or the alumni office at [official contact]. Don’t share sensitive personal details in DMs.”

Step 6: Safe replies to sketchy requests
- “I only share personal details through official channels. Please provide the organizer’s contact at [school/alumni org] so I can confirm.”
- “Can we jump on a quick call or video chat? I want to be sure I’m speaking with the right person.”
- “What was the last class or event we attended together?” (A real friend can answer easily.)

Step 7: If you encounter an impersonation attempt
- Take screenshots of the profile, messages, and links.
- Report the account on the platform and block it.
- Alert the real friend and mutual contacts that a clone account may be active.
- If you clicked a link or shared data, update passwords, enable two-factor authentication, and monitor accounts for unusual activity.

This approach equips you to recognize and avoid social engineering while modeling how a genuine organizer would communicate without soliciting sensitive data.
